episodes.215414: A backdoor front pushed through eastern New Mexico during the morning hours of August 19th resulting in an uptick in thunderstorm activity across the higher terrain and nearby lower elevations of central New Mexico. Thunderstorms producing locally heavy rainfall resulted in debris flow in and below the 2024 South Fork burn scar. Severe thunderstorms also produced large hail along the eastern slopes of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains and severe wind gust in the Sevilleta National Wildlife Refuge.
episodes.215420: During the morning and into the early afternoon hours of August 20, 2026, multiple hours of moderate-to-heavy rainfall across saturated areas of Clearfield and Centre Counties brought multiple instances of flash flooding. The majority of flash flooding during the morning and afternoon hours was limited to water covering roadways and water rushing into basements across the area. Showers and storms began to intensify across southeastern Pennsylvania, where ample shear (especially in the 0-1km layer) and instability was available. An isolated thunderstorm across portions of Adams County began to cause isolated instances of tree damage before pushing into an environment where low-level shear continued to increase. This increase in low-level shear allowed for four tornadoes to spawn, one in York County with three in Lancaster County. The most considerable damage occurred when an EF-2 tornado fully ripped off multiple sections of roofing and bricks were shifted from their original location at the top of the auditorium, where the roof was also ripped off.
episodes.215501: On the 19th afternoon to overnight, the active mid-August pattern brought another round of thunderstorms and locally heavy rain across central Indiana.  Despite only near-normal warmth and dewpoints, a train of multiple upper short wave troughs flowing west to east over the Midwest, around a deep 500 mb low near James Bay, promoted training downpours and occasional rotating cells.  Main activity trended from multiple rounds of numerous cells over far northern zones through afternoon and early evening hours, down through the Interstate 70 corridor later in the evening, to an early overnight resurgence of strong/severe cells from west-central to southeastern central Indiana.||Flash flooding was the primary impact, in areas where an additional 3.00-4.50 inches of rain fell;  in the evening from the Lafayette area to Madison County, and later in the overnight in mainly Putnam County.  Overall isolated damaging winds were focused in the evening from Tipton to Delaware County and briefly during the overnight in Putnam County.  Large hail, up to 1.50 inches, and a very brief EF-U tornado were both confined to a cell crossing Delaware County around 1630 EST.

episodes.215577: Supercells and line segments developed as a Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV) passed along a warm front. The storms became most organized as they crossed the Chesapeake Bay, but sporadic severe weather occurred over parts of northern Virginia to north-central Maryland.

episodes.216178: A stationary frontal boundary interacted with a moist airmass to produce thunderstorms with heavy rainfall during the evening of August 19th.  As a result, a narrow corridor of flash flooding was observed from Tazewell County eastward to Champaign County.
episodes.216226: A prefrontal trough developed along the Coastal Plain of North Carolina during the afternoon hours of August twentieth out ahead of an incoming cold front which remained well to the west during the day. Along this prefrontal trough, linear segments of scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across far western portions of eastern North Carolina and the Triad vicinity with this activity pushing east through the afternoon and evening. With ample instability in place, a few of these storms became severe in nature bringing a strong wind threat to portions of the inland rivers of Eastern North Carolina. Shower and thunderstorm activity then quickly weakened after sunset as instability quickly lowered with the loss of daytime heating.
episodes.216247: A cold front approached from the northwest into Ohio on the morning of August 20th, then sank southeastward across the area by the end of the day. Precipitation accompanying the front deposited one to three inches of rain across portions of Perry, Morgan, and Washington Counties. This led to flooded roads, water rescues around Buckeye Lake, and river flooding on Duck Creek and the Muskingum River.

episodes.216436: A cold front moved from the NW to SE across Minnesota with a threat for severe weather mostly across the central portion of the state. However, enhanced clearing across southwest MN led to efficient atmospheric recovery from precipitation that had moved through earlier in the day. By the early evening, storms redeveloped along the frontal boundary and moved into a buoyant sheared airmass. This resulted in isolated cells to feature rotating updrafts and produce quarter to tennis ball size hail across portions of southwestern MN. ||The tennis ball size hail stone (2.5 diameter) was measured near the border of Yellow Medicine and Redwood Counties or 4 miles NE of Vesta.
episodes.216578: A line of scattered showers and storms developed along and east of the Triangle region, over the eastern Piedmont, Sandhills, and Coastal Plain during the afternoon and early evening. Several storms became severe with numerous trees and powerlines reported down in Nash, Johnston, Wilson, and Cumberland Counties.
episodes.216825: A large cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the early evening hours on the 19th along the higher terrain and foothills east of the Phoenix Metro Area. These thunderstorms were fueled by strong instability as MLCAPE values ranged between 1500-2000 J/KG along with similarly high DCAPE values, making the environment very conducive for strong downburst winds and thus strong outflows. The thunderstorm complex generated a large outflow boundary that propagated west-northwestward through the entire Phoenix area. The boundary produced a widespread swath of damaging straight-line winds gusts ranging between 55 to 65 mph as detected the doppler radar and measured by surface weather stations. Additionally, the outflow boundary generated a significant dust storm, reducing visibility to less than one mile across multiple locations. There were even some areas, as evidenced by the webcams operated by the Arizona Department of Transportation, in which visibilities dropped under a quarter-mile, particularly in the Phoenix East Valley. Due to wind gusts exceeding 60 mph, multiple reports of storm damage were received, which predominantly consisted of downed or damaged trees. Partial structural roof damage was also reported in localized areas, with the most severe impact observed at Marcos De Niza High School in Tempe, where several roof sections sustained damage.

episodes.217591: During the early afternoon of August 19th, a lingering surface boundary and rapidly developing thunderstorms interacted, producing several pronounced funnel clouds in far western Iowa. A remnant outflow boundary helped to initiate several weak thunderstorms in western Iowa during the evening of October 19th. These thunderstorms produced several instances of pronounced and highly-visible funnel clouds. No touchdowns or damage was reported with any of these reports.

episodes.217603: On Thursday, August 20, 2026, an advancing frontal system triggered scattered rounds of severe thunderstorms across north-central and northeastern Minnesota. As these cells intensified during the late afternoon and evening, they produced frequent lightning and numerous reports of quarter- to half-dollar-sized hail across counties including Cass, Crow Wing, Aitkin, and Itasca. Communities such as Boy River, Remer, and areas near Crosslake and Silica were directly hit by localized hail swaths and brief downpours. In addition to the hail activity, gusty downdrafts knocked down trees and caused minor home damage near Brainerd before storms tracked further south and east.
episodes.217714: A shortwave over northeast Kansas and northwest Missouri approached the Mid-South during the early morning hours on August 20th. A low-level jet began to ramp up and bring a 60kt maxima across southern Kentucky. With this jet ramping up, robust nocturnal convection was able to produce damaging winds, downing trees across the Mid-South as 2 PWATs, moderately steep lapse rates, and MLCAPE values between 1500-2500 J/kg were present. Severe storms also struck in the afternoon hours as DCAPE values surged to around 1000 J/kg, resulting in wet microbursts and damaging winds.

episodes.217724: A weak quasi-stationary mid-level boundary extending from central Mississippi down to coastal Mississippi and Alabama served as a focusing mechanism for a broken line of storms to form across the Pine Belt region of Mississippi in the late afternoon and early evening hours.  These storms then moved to the south-southwest and produced localized damaging wind gusts in coastal and southwest Mississippi.
episodes.217823: On August 18th, weak shortwave energy moved through the eastern periphery of the Heat Wave ridge over a moist and unstable airmass enhancing storms mainly over northeast and central Florida. Scattered showers and storms developed along the inland-moving sea breezes with stronger storms, capable of wet microbursts, pulsing along mesoscale boundary collisions in the afternoon into evening. On August 19-20, a frontal boundary stalled over southern Georgia as ���Heat Wave��� ridging built in from the west. Tropical moisture of 2+ inches of precipitable water remained south of the front, mainly over northeast Florida. Scattered showers and storms developed along the inland-moving sea breezes. The combination of high moisture, strong diurnal heating, and sea breeze/outflow interactions supported strong to severe storms capable of producing damaging winds, frequent lightning strikes and torrential downpours. Weak steering flow allowed for localized flooding. On August 22nd, lingering upper shortwaves ahead of the weakening frontal boundary in central Georgia triggered morning showers and isolated storms moving inland from the Gulf. Convection then spread east-northeastward through the day in the general southwest flow. A few stronger storms occurred along sea breeze boundary mergers in the late morning to early afternoon hours in north-central Florida.
episodes.217886: A band of showers and thunderstorms developed along and south of the highway 60 corridor on the afternoon of the 20th in the Texas Panhandle. Thunderstorms started off weak and pulse-like, but they eventually became organized for a few strong storms and one severe storm in Randall and Deaf Smith county.

episodes.218167: During the late afternoon and early evening hours on August 20th, thunderstorms quickly developed along and near a stationary boundary draped across Southeast Oklahoma and Southwest Arkansas. Along and south of the boundary, temperatures soared near 105 degrees with lower to middle 60s dewpoints, resulting in a strongly unstable air mass. This activity was largely displaced from a mid-level trough and more enhanced flow aloft moving across the lower Ohio Valley, limiting the overall scope of convective organization. Nevertheless, near 25 knots of mid-level northwesterly flow oriented perpendicular to the stationary boundary and evolving thunderstorms supported a more loosely organized cluster of storms capable of producing locally damaging wind gusts. As a result, several reports of wind damage were recorded across parts of Southwest Arkansas.
episodes.218284: A very warm and unstable airmass was in place across the Mid-Atlantic on August 20. A disturbance aloft passed by to the north but was able to spark several rounds of strong storms across Virginia with strong winds and frequent lightning.

The West Fork Duck Creek at Macksburg exceeded a bankfull level of 13 feet on the afternoon of August 20th. The creek continued to rise to a crest near 14.8 feet the next morning and then receded below bankfull again that evening. Impacts while the creek was out of its banks included flooding of Broad Street, Main Street, fields along the creek, and the campground next to the gauge.

A 66 year-old female was indirectly struck by lightning when walking outside. The  lightning struck a nearby generator area and then by either a side flash or ground  current indirectly caused burn injuries to the victims hands and feet. The time of the event was based on the victim's report and archived lightning data. The cost of lightning damage was unknown, but her generator was a complete loss.
A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 70 mph snapped multiple trees just east of Chimney Rock peak.

An EF-2 tornado occurred in eastern York County, PA on August 20th, 2026 with a path length of 1.07 miles and a path width of 100 yards. The tornado began to cause damage north of Samuel S. Lewis State park and moved east-southeast to Eastern York High School. This is where the most significant damage occurred; parts of the roof was uplifted and some walls collapsed bringing peak wind speed up to 120mph. The tornado continued producing weaker damage another quarter mile east of the high school. Sidings and roofs of houses were damaged with wind speeds around 90-95mph. An injury occurred at one of these houses where the windows where blown in. The tornado continued into a field, causing some crop damage. This was mostly in the form of corn being blown down at 70-80mph with some debris landing in the field. The tornado lifted in this field.
A severe thunderstorm, producing winds estimated near 70mph, knocked down multiple large oak trees down. Aluminum siding debris was found in a yard.

An EF-1 tornado occurred in western Lancaster County, PA with a path length of 3.01 miles and a path width of 100 yards. The tornado touched down in Columbia, causing roof and brick wall damage to low-rise buildings with wind speeds around 90mph. Despite prevailing easterly storm motion, the tornado exhibited anomalous motion from northwest to southeast as it left Columbia, paralleling the Susquehanna River. This portion of its path is when the tornado caused its most intense damage at around 100mph, snapping multiple trees. Around Shultz Road, the tornado took on a more easterly turn and weakened in intensity. The tornado twisted and broke branches with wind speeds around 70mph. It lifted in a cornfield a minute later.
A severe thunderstorm, producing estimated wind gusts near 60mph, broke small hardwood limbs off their parent trees near Charlestown Road.
A few shingles were blown off a roof, and many large tree branches down near Laurel Lake Road.
A severe thunderstorm, producing wind gusts estimated near 60 mph knocked a tree down across Millersville Road.

An EF-0 tornado occurred near Habecker Church Road, east of Lancaster PA. It had a path length of 0.3 miles  and path width of 75 yards. The estimated  maximum wind speed was 65 mph. It touched down north of Habecker Church Road and blew down some corn in a field before moving south. It crossed Habecker Church Road and continued crop damage until the tornado lifted in another corn field.
Trees downed and damage to homes occured in Ecru, MS.

An EF-0 Tornado occurred east of Lancaster, PA, with a path length of 0.49 miles and path width 125 yards. The tornado began to cause damage in Woods Edge subdivision with wind speeds of 80-85mph. Multiple trees were uprooted and some condominiums had portions of their rooves blown off. The tornado continued east into a wooded area where it broke off multiple large branches of a tree with wind speeds of 80mph before lifting.
